UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
O R D E R
A.  PRELIMINARY
1. This batch of writ petitions and contempt petitions arises out
of the prohibitory orders and restrictions imposed in the National
Capital Territory of Delhi in October 2026, in connection with a
protest proposed to be held at Jantar Mantar on 10.10.2026, and the
events  that  followed.  W.P.(C)  Nos.  1373/2026,  1406/2026  and
1395/2026 (Item Nos. 20, 21 and 23), which are listed today as
fresh matters, raise allied issues and are taken up along with this
batch.
2. By our order dated 15.10.2026, Ms. Aarthi Rajan and Mr. Bhuvan
Kapoor, learned counsel, were appointed as Nodal Counsel on behalf
of the petitioners and the respondents, respectively. They were
requested to segregate the cases into broad categories, so that a
separate and comprehensive counter affidavit may be filed in
respect of each group.
18

--- Page 42 ---
3. In compliance therewith, Ms. Aarthi Rajan, learned Nodal
Counsel for the petitioners, at the outset, informed us that the
matters forming part of this batch have been categorised, and that
such categorisation, in a tabulated form, has been furnished to the
office of the learned Solicitor General of India. A similar
categorisation of documents has also been furnished to us by Mr.
Bhuvan Kapoor, learned Nodal Counsel for the respondents. Revised
categorisations, both dated 03.11.2026, have also been filed by
each of the learned Nodal Counsel. The same are taken on record.
4. The two categorisations are, in substance, identical. They
account for the same thirty-three matters and place each of them
under the same head, save in one respect. The categorisation filed
on behalf of the petitioners treats the petition concerning women
journalists and the petition concerning police personnel as two
distinct categories, whereas the categorisation filed on behalf of
the respondents groups them under a single head. Since the two
petitions arise from a common factual setting but seek distinct
reliefs, we deem it appropriate to place them under one category,
with two sub-categories.
5. The matters shall, accordingly, stand categorised as follows:
1. Main Writ Petition and Contempt Petitions;
2. Challenge to the de-notification of Jantar Mantar as
a protest site;
3. Petitions concerning detention/removal;
4. Petitions challenging restrictions on protests;
4.1 Petitions challenging the order(s) issued under
Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha 
Sanhita, 2023 ("BNSS");
19

--- Page 43 ---
5. Petitions concerning journalists;
6. Petitions concerning women journalists and police 
personnel;
6.1 Petition concerning women journalists;
6.2 Petition concerning police personnel;
7. Petitions concerning lawyers;
8. Petitions seeking regulation of protests;
9. Habeas Corpus;
10. Challenge to the vires of Section 172 of the BNSS; 
and
11. Petition concerning surveillance.
B.  CLARIFICATION OF PARAGRAPH 16(e) OF THE ORDER DATED 11.10.2026
6. Before proceeding, we deem it appropriate to clarify paragraph
16(e) of the order dated 11.10.2026 passed in Contempt Petition
(Civil) Diary No. 63801/2026, since registered as Contempt Petition
(Civil)  No.  844/2026.  Vide  that  direction,  the  authorities
concerned were asked to take down a notice board, put up in the
Supreme Court premises, stating that Section 163 of the BNSS had
been invoked in and around the precincts of this Court.
7. The said direction was issued for the limited purpose of
securing unhindered ingress to and egress from this Court and other
Courts of law. Its object was to ensure that access to justice was
not impeded, and that no Advocate, litigant, or person visiting an
Advocate for professional consultation, was obstructed or deterred.
It did not stay, suspend or otherwise dilute any prohibitory order
issued under Section 163 of the BNSS, the validity whereof is the
subject matter of W.P.(Crl.) Nos. 427/2026 and 429/2026, pending
before us.
20

--- Page 44 ---
8. It has been brought to our notice that the said direction is
being misconstrued, and is being misused by certain elements, as
though it had lifted the prohibitory order(s) in the Supreme Court
premises.  
9. We, therefore, recall paragraph 16(e) of our order dated
11.10.2026  and  clarify  that  nothing  contained  therein  shall
preclude the Competent Authority from displaying the notice afresh,
subject to the condition that the free movement of Advocates,
litigants and other persons having business before this Court, or
any other Court, is properly regulated and not obstructed in any
manner. 
C.  GENERAL DIRECTIONS
10. The matters shall henceforth be listed and heard category-
wise, in the sequence set out hereinabove. The respondents may
separately file their counter-affidavits or responses for each
category.
11. To facilitate an orderly and effective hearing, learned Senior
Counsel and counsel appearing in each category must coordinate
through the respective Nodal Counsel and submit, in advance of the
next date of hearing, the time they propose to take for oral
arguments. Learned counsel espousing a common cause within a
category are expected to avoid duplication of submissions.
12. Pending interlocutory applications in each matter shall be
taken up along with the category to which that matter belongs.
21

--- Page 45 ---

UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
O R D E R
A.  PRELIMINARY
1. This batch of writ petitions and contempt petitions arises out
of the prohibitory orders and restrictions imposed in the National
Capital Territory of Delhi in October 2026, in connection with a
protest proposed to be held at Jantar Mantar on 10.10.2026, and the
events  that  followed.  W.P.(C)  Nos.  1373/2026,  1406/2026  and
1395/2026 (Item Nos. 20, 21 and 23), which are listed today as
fresh matters, raise allied issues and are taken up along with this
batch.
2. By our order dated 15.10.2026, Ms. Aarthi Rajan and Mr. Bhuvan
Kapoor, learned counsel, were appointed as Nodal Counsel on behalf
of the petitioners and the respondents, respectively. They were
requested to segregate the cases into broad categories, so that a
separate and comprehensive counter affidavit may be filed in
respect of each group.
3. In compliance therewith, Ms. Aarthi Rajan, learned Nodal
Counsel for the petitioners, at the outset, informed us that the
matters forming part of this batch have been categorised, and that
44

--- Page 68 ---
such categorisation, in a tabulated form, has been furnished to the
office of the learned Solicitor General of India. A similar
categorisation of documents has also been furnished to us by Mr.
Bhuvan Kapoor, learned Nodal Counsel for the respondents. Revised
categorisations, both dated 03.11.2026, have also been filed by
each of the learned Nodal Counsel. The same are taken on record.
4. The two categorisations are, in substance, identical. They
account for the same thirty-three matters and place each of them
under the same head, save in one respect. The categorisation filed
on behalf of the petitioners treats the petition concerning women
journalists and the petition concerning police personnel as two
distinct categories, whereas the categorisation filed on behalf of
the respondents groups them under a single head. Since the two
petitions arise from a common factual setting but seek distinct
reliefs, we deem it appropriate to place them under one category,
with two sub-categories.
5. The matters shall, accordingly, stand categorised as follows:
1. Main Writ Petition and Contempt Petitions;
2. Challenge to the de-notification of Jantar Mantar as
a protest site;
3. Petitions concerning detention/removal;
4. Petitions challenging restrictions on protests;
4.1 Petitions challenging the order(s) issued under
Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha 
Sanhita, 2023 ("BNSS");
5. Petitions concerning journalists;
6. Petitions concerning women journalists and police 
personnel;
6.1 Petition concerning women journalists;
45

--- Page 69 ---
6.2 Petition concerning police personnel;
7. Petitions concerning lawyers;
8. Petitions seeking regulation of protests;
9. Habeas Corpus;
10. Challenge to the vires of Section 172 of the BNSS; 
and
11. Petition concerning surveillance.
B.  CLARIFICATION OF PARAGRAPH 16(e) OF THE ORDER DATED 11.10.2026
6. Before proceeding, we deem it appropriate to clarify paragraph
16(e) of the order dated 11.10.2026 passed in Contempt Petition
(Civil) Diary No. 63801/2026, since registered as Contempt Petition
(Civil)  No.  844/2026.  Vide  that  direction,  the  authorities
concerned were asked to take down a notice board, put up in the
Supreme Court premises, stating that Section 163 of the BNSS had
been invoked in and around the precincts of this Court.
7. The said direction was issued for the limited purpose of
securing unhindered ingress to and egress from this Court and other
Courts of law. Its object was to ensure that access to justice was
not impeded, and that no Advocate, litigant, or person visiting an
Advocate for professional consultation, was obstructed or deterred.
It did not stay, suspend or otherwise dilute any prohibitory order
issued under Section 163 of the BNSS, the validity whereof is the
subject matter of W.P.(Crl.) Nos. 427/2026 and 429/2026, pending
before us.
8. It has been brought to our notice that the said direction is
being misconstrued, and is being misused by certain elements, as
46

--- Page 70 ---
though it had lifted the prohibitory order(s) in the Supreme Court
premises.  
9. We, therefore, recall paragraph 16(e) of our order dated
11.10.2026  and  clarify  that  nothing  contained  therein  shall
preclude the Competent Authority from displaying the notice afresh,
subject to the condition that the free movement of Advocates,
litigants and other persons having business before this Court, or
any other Court, is properly regulated and not obstructed in any
manner. 
C.  GENERAL DIRECTIONS
10. The matters shall henceforth be listed and heard category-
wise, in the sequence set out hereinabove. The respondents may
separately file their counter-affidavits or responses for each
category.
11. To facilitate an orderly and effective hearing, learned Senior
Counsel and counsel appearing in each category must coordinate
through the respective Nodal Counsel and submit, in advance of the
next date of hearing, the time they propose to take for oral
arguments. Learned counsel espousing a common cause within a
category are expected to avoid duplication of submissions.
12. Pending interlocutory applications in each matter shall be
taken up along with the category to which that matter belongs.

UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
O R D E R
A.  PRELIMINARY
1. This batch of writ petitions and contempt petitions arises out
of the prohibitory orders and restrictions imposed in the National
Capital Territory of Delhi in October 2026, in connection with a
protest proposed to be held at Jantar Mantar on 10.10.2026, and the
events  that  followed.  W.P.(C)  Nos.  1373/2026,  1406/2026  and
1395/2026 (Item Nos. 20, 21 and 23), which are listed today as
fresh matters, raise allied issues and are taken up along with this
batch.
2. By our order dated 15.10.2026, Ms. Aarthi Rajan and Mr. Bhuvan
Kapoor, learned counsel, were appointed as Nodal Counsel on behalf
of the petitioners and the respondents, respectively. They were
requested to segregate the cases into broad categories, so that a
separate and comprehensive counter affidavit may be filed in
respect of each group.
3. In compliance therewith, Ms. Aarthi Rajan, learned Nodal
Counsel for the petitioners, at the outset, informed us that the
matters forming part of this batch have been categorised, and that
18

--- Page 130 ---
such categorisation, in a tabulated form, has been furnished to the
office of the learned Solicitor General of India. A similar
categorisation of documents has also been furnished to us by Mr.
Bhuvan Kapoor, learned Nodal Counsel for the respondents. Revised
categorisations, both dated 03.11.2026, have also been filed by
each of the learned Nodal Counsel. The same are taken on record.
4. The two categorisations are, in substance, identical. They
account for the same thirty-three matters and place each of them
under the same head, save in one respect. The categorisation filed
on behalf of the petitioners treats the petition concerning women
journalists and the petition concerning police personnel as two
distinct categories, whereas the categorisation filed on behalf of
the respondents groups them under a single head. Since the two
petitions arise from a common factual setting but seek distinct
reliefs, we deem it appropriate to place them under one category,
with two sub-categories.
5. The matters shall, accordingly, stand categorised as follows:
1. Main Writ Petition and Contempt Petitions;
2. Challenge to the de-notification of Jantar Mantar as
a protest site;
3. Petitions concerning detention/removal;
4. Petitions challenging restrictions on protests;
4.1 Petitions challenging the order(s) issued under
Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha 
Sanhita, 2023 ("BNSS");
5. Petitions concerning journalists;
6. Petitions concerning women journalists and police 
personnel;
6.1 Petition concerning women journalists;
19

--- Page 131 ---
6.2 Petition concerning police personnel;
7. Petitions concerning lawyers;
8. Petitions seeking regulation of protests;
9. Habeas Corpus;
10. Challenge to the vires of Section 172 of the BNSS; 
and
11. Petition concerning surveillance.
B.  CLARIFICATION OF PARAGRAPH 16(e) OF THE ORDER DATED 11.10.2026
6. Before proceeding, we deem it appropriate to clarify paragraph
16(e) of the order dated 11.10.2026 passed in Contempt Petition
(Civil) Diary No. 63801/2026, since registered as Contempt Petition
(Civil)  No.  844/2026.  Vide  that  direction,  the  authorities
concerned were asked to take down a notice board, put up in the
Supreme Court premises, stating that Section 163 of the BNSS had
been invoked in and around the precincts of this Court.
7. The said direction was issued for the limited purpose of
securing unhindered ingress to and egress from this Court and other
Courts of law. Its object was to ensure that access to justice was
not impeded, and that no Advocate, litigant, or person visiting an
Advocate for professional consultation, was obstructed or deterred.
It did not stay, suspend or otherwise dilute any prohibitory order
issued under Section 163 of the BNSS, the validity whereof is the
subject matter of W.P.(Crl.) Nos. 427/2026 and 429/2026, pending
before us.
8. It has been brought to our notice that the said direction is
being misconstrued, and is being misused by certain elements, as
20

--- Page 132 ---
though it had lifted the prohibitory order(s) in the Supreme Court
premises.  
9. We, therefore, recall paragraph 16(e) of our order dated
11.10.2026  and  clarify  that  nothing  contained  therein  shall
preclude the Competent Authority from displaying the notice afresh,
subject to the condition that the free movement of Advocates,
litigants and other persons having business before this Court, or
any other Court, is properly regulated and not obstructed in any
manner. 
C.  GENERAL DIRECTIONS
10. The matters shall henceforth be listed and heard category-
wise, in the sequence set out hereinabove. The respondents may
separately file their counter-affidavits or responses for each
category.
11. To facilitate an orderly and effective hearing, learned Senior
Counsel and counsel appearing in each category must coordinate
through the respective Nodal Counsel and submit, in advance of the
next date of hearing, the time they propose to take for oral
arguments. Learned counsel espousing a common cause within a
category are expected to avoid duplication of submissions.
12. Pending interlocutory applications in each matter shall be
taken up along with the category to which that matter belongs.

Leave granted.
2. Briefly stated, the facts of the case are that the appellant
herein was booked for the murder of Janmejay, Pappu and Muma

Azamgarh  was  not  supported  by  any  reliable  documentary

1 
      IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
    CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
 
 
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.________ OF 2026 
(Arising out of Special Leave to Appeal 
(Crl.) No. 18612/2026) 
 
 
 
RAMEELA W/O LATE MAHENDRA             APPELLANT(S) 
 
 
 
                           VERSUS 
 
 
 
STATE OF RAJASTHAN & ANR.            RESPONDENT(S) 
 
 
 
 
 
 
     O R D E R 
 
 
1. Leave granted. 
2. This appeal is at the instance of the de facto 
complainant-wife of the deceased being dissatisfied 
with the impugned judgment and order passed by the 
High Court dated 18.5.2026 in Criminal Appeal No. 253 
of 2024, by which the High Court partly allowed the 

--- Page 151 ---
 
2 
criminal appeal preferred by the respondent            
no.2 (original accused) before us by altering the 
conviction for the offence punishable under Section 
302 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (for short “the 
IPC”) to Section 304 Part II of the IPC. 
3. To put it briefly, the respondent-accused was put 
to trial in the Court of Special Judge, Scheduled 
Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of 
Atrocities), Act in Special Case No. 50 of 2021 for 
the offence punishable under Section 302 of the IPC 
and Section 3(2)(v) of the Scheduled Castes and the 
Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities)  Act, 
1989, respectively. 
4. It is the case of the prosecution that, on the 
date of the incident, the respondent -accused armed 
with a knife, came at  the house of the deceased and 
picked up an altercation.  In the course of the 
altercation, the respondent -accused is alleged to 
have inflicted stab wounds on the deceased. 

--- Page 152 ---
 
3 
5. The deceased was immediately shifted to the 
hospital and he succumbed to the injuries after a 
period of 16 days while he was undergoing treatment 
in the hospital.  
6. There are eyewitnesses to the incident. 
7. The Trial Court at the end of the trial held the 
respondent-accused guilty of the alleged crime and 
convicted him for murder.  The respondent-accused was 
sentenced to undergo life imprisonment with fine. 
8. The respondent -accused being dissatisfied, with 
the judgment and order of conviction passed by the 
Trial Court, went in appeal before the High Court.  
The High Court took the view that since the deceased 
succumbed to the stab injuries after a period of 16 
days, the same would be indicative of the fact that 
the respondent -accused had no intention to cause 
death of the deceased.  To put it in another words, 
the judgment of the High Court could also be 
understood trying to convey that the cause of death 

--- Page 153 ---
 
4 
as assigned in the post -mortem is septicemia and 
septicemia cannot be said to be the direct result of 
the injuries suffered by the deceased at the time of 
assault.   
9. The wife of the deceased -original complainant 
being dissatisfied with the impugned judgment and 
order passed by the High Court is here before us with 
the present appeal. 
10. We heard the learned counsel appearing for the 
parties. 
11. The short point for our consideration is whether 
the High Court was justified in altering the 
conviction from Section 302 to Section 304 Part II of 
the IPC? 
12. We are of the view that the High Court committed 
an egregious error in passing the impugned judgment 
and order altering the conviction.  The issue in 
question has been settled by this Court in its 
decision in Maniklal Sahu vs. State of Chhattisgarh 

--- Page 154 ---
 
5 
reported in 2025 SCC OnLine SC 1960. 
13. The paragraph  no. 69  of Maniklal Sahu  (supra) 
reads thus:- 
“69. We may highlight few broad principles 
that the courts must keep in mind. 
 
a. If it is proved that the injury was 
fatal and the intention was to cause 
death, though the death occurred after 
several days of septicaemia or other 
complications having supervened, yet it is 
undoubtedly a murder as it falls within 
the first limb of Section 300 of the IPC.  
b. If it is proved that the injuries by 
themselves were sufficient to cause death 
in the ordinary course of nature, and if 
it is established that those injuries were 
the intended injuries, though the death 
might have occurred after septicaemia or 
other complications had supervened, yet 
the act of the accused would squarely fall 
under the third limb of Section 300 of the 
IPC and the accused is therefore liable to 
be punished under Section 302 of the IPC.  
c. If it is proved that the injuries were 
imminently dangerous to life, though the 
death had occurred after septicaemia or 
other complications had supervened, yet 
the act of the accused would squarely fall 
under the fourth limb of Section 300 of 
the IPC, provided, the other requirements 
like knowledge on the part of the accused, 
etc. are satisfied and so the accused 

--- Page 155 ---
 
6 
would be liable to be punished under 
Section 302 of the IPC. Here also, the 
primary cause of the death is the injuries 
and septicaemia.  
d. In judging whether the injuries 
inflicted were sufficient in the ordinary 
course of nature to cause death, the 
possibility that skilful and efficient 
medical treatment might prevent the fatal 
result is wholly irrelevant.  
e. If the supervening causes are 
attributable to the injuries caused, then 
the person inflicting the injuries is 
liable for causing death, even if death 
was not the direct result of the injuries.  
f. Broadly speaking, the courts would have 
to undertake the exercise to distinguish 
between two types of cases; first, where 
the intervening cause of death, like 
peritonitis, is only a remote and a rather 
improbable consequence of the injury; then 
it can be said that the injury is one 
which may, in particular circumstances, 
result in death, but which may not in 
ordinary course of nature be likely to 
lead to it. Secondly, where the 
complication which is the intervening 
cause of death is itself a practically 
inevitable sequence to the injury. In that 
event, the probability is very high  
indeed, amounting to practical certainty 
i.e., death is a result in due course of 
natural events. A deep abdominal thrust 
with a knife followed by injury to the 
internal organs is practically certain to 
result in acute peritonitis causing death. 
It is clearly a case of murder under 

--- Page 156 ---
 
7 
Section 302 and not merely of culpable 
homicide.  
g. Even when the medical evidence does not 
say that any one of the injuries on the 
body of the deceased was sufficient to 
cause death in the ordinary course of 
nature, yet it is open to the Court to 
look into the nature of the injuries found 
on the body of the deceased and infer from 
them that the assailants intended to cause 
death of the deceased. If none of the 
injuries alone were sufficient in the 
ordinary course of nature to cause the 
death of the deceased, cumulatively, they 
may be sufficient in the or dinary course 
of nature to cause his death.  
h. What the courts must see is whether the 
injuries were sufficient in the ordinary 
course of nature to cause death, or to 
cause such bodily injuries as the accused 
knew to be likely to cause death although 
death was ultimately due to supervention 
of some other cause. An intervening cause 
or complication is by itself not of such 
significance. What is significant is 
whether death was only a remote 
possibility, or is one which would have 
occurred in due course.  
i. To sum it up, where death is delayed 
due to later complications or 
developments, the courts should consider 
the nature of the injury, complications or 
the attending circumstances. If the 
complications or developments are the 
natural, or probable, or necessary 
consequence of the injury, and if it is 
reasonably contemplated as its result, the 

--- Page 157 ---
 
8 
injury could be said to have caused death. 
If on the other hand, the chain of 
consequences is broken, or if there is 
unexpected complication causing new 
mischief, the relation of cause and effect 
is not established, or the causal 
connection is too remote then the injury 
cannot be said to have caused death. If 
the original injury itself is of a fatal 
nature, it makes no difference that death 
is actually caused  by a complication 
naturally flowing from the injury and not 
the injury itself, since causal connection 
is proximate.” 
 
14. Thus, it goes without saying that if the cause of 
death was septicemia, the same was a result of 
nothing but the stab wounds that  the deceased 
suffered at the hands of the respondent-accused. 
15. The cause of death could be said to be the direct 
result of the injuries suffered by the deceased and, 
therefore, it is a case of murder punishable under 
Section 302 of the IPC. 
16. In view of the aforesaid, the appeal succeeds and 
is hereby allowed.  The judgment and order of the 
High Court is set aside.  The original judgment and 

--- Page 158 ---
 
9 
order of conviction and sentence passed by the Trial 
Court is restored. 
17. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand 
disposed of. 
 
...................J. 
         [J.B. PARDIWALA] 
        
 
 
      ...................J.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA 
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION 
 
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO. 2804 OF 2025 
 
DINESHA U.N. & ANR.                     …APPELLANT(S) 
VERSUS 
 
STATE OF KARNATAKA                                   …RESPONDENT(S) 
 
ORDER 
          Leave has been granted vide order dated 16th May 2025. 
2. The appellants are aggrieved by the judgment dated  
17th January 2024 rendered in Criminal Appeal No. 1603/2017(C) by 
which the judgment of conviction and the order of sentence both dated 
1st April 2017 passed in SC No. 115 of 2015 have been affirmed by the 
High Court. 
3. Dinesha U.N. and Manukumara were convicted and sentenced 
to life imprisonment and a fine of Rs.10,000/- each under section 302 
read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code with a default 
stipulation of RI for One year for committing murder of Mahendra. 
They were further convicted and sentenced to RI for Seven years with 
a fine of Rs.5,000 each under section 30 7 read with section 34 of 
Indian Penal Code  with a default stipulation of SI for One year and 
under section 341 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code for 

--- Page 171 ---
 
Page 2 of 8 
 
which they were sentenced of SI for One year and a fine of Rs.500 
each with a default stipulation of SI for 10 days.  
4. On the basis of a complaint which was lodged by Nanjegowda, 
Crime No. 175 of 2014 was registered on 11th November 2014 against 
Dinesha U.N. , Manukumara and Smt.  Rathnamma under sections 
341 and 307 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code. Mahendra 
who is the son of the informant succumbed to the injury caused to 
him by the accused persons on 10th November 2014 and, accordingly, 
the offence under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal 
Code was added in the Report. In support of the charges framed on 
2nd February 2016 against the accused persons under sections 341, 
307 and 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code , the 
prosecution produced 20 witnesses. PW1 Nan jegowda and PW2 
Sarojamma are the parents of Mahendra and PW5 is the real brother 
of Mahendra. Two other witnesses, namely, PW3 and PW4 are also 
close relatives of Mahendra.  As PW14, Dr. P.I. Inamdar who 
conducted the post -mortem examination  gave a description of the 
external injuries found on the dead body of Mahendra. On 
examination, he found the following external injuries: 
“1. Swelling present over the left cheek area. 
2. Abrasion measuring 3 X 1.5 cm present over the left frontal eminence. 
3. Abrasion measuring 5 X 2cm, present over the upper part of neck 
below the mandible. 
4. Abrasion measuring 2 X 1cm present over the upper part of chest 11cm 
medial and above right nipple. 

--- Page 172 ---
 
Page 3 of 8 
 
5. Abrasion measuring 3 X 3cm, pre sent over the lower 1/3 of left 
forearm. 
6. Bleeding from the left angle of mouth.” 
 
 On dissection of the skull, the doctor  found the following 
internal injuries: 
"Scalp, Skull Meninges and brain and Vertebra: Circular shaped contusion 
covering 21X14cm, present over the parieto -temporal and occipital area, 
Subdural haematoma measuring 16X2X14cm, covering left temporal and 
occipital region, Depressed fracture covering 5X5cm, present over the left 
parietal bond (both tables), continued as suture fracture lin e (14cm) 
ending 1cm in front of foramen magnum, Brain oedematous and soft, 
diffused suborchonoid haemorrhage." 
 
5. Both the appellants are close relatives; Dinesha U.N. is the 
cousin brother of Manukumara. This is the admitted position that 
Smt. Rathnamma who is the mother of Manukumara and was also 
convicted for committing murder of Mahendra succeeded before the 
High Court and her conviction and sentence under section 302 read 
with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code were set aside  but the High 
Court maintained the conviction of the appellants for the offence of 
murder. For convicting the appellants, the High Court relied on the 
testimony of prosecution witnesses and held that the prosecution was 
successful in establishing the charges framed against them. Both the 
Courts took note of the alternative plea raised on behalf of the 
appellants that they were not liable to be convicted under section 302 
read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and at be st their case 

--- Page 173 ---
 
Page 4 of 8 
 
falls under Exception-4 to section 300 of the Indian Penal Code.  The 
High Court dealt with this plea as under:- 
“31. Further, the trial Court was justified in holding that the accused 
attempted to commit murder of PW1 and committed the murder  of 
Mahendra by inflicting him homicidal injuries. Having regard to the 
fact that accused Nos.1 and 2 assaulted the victim with deadly 
weapons MOs.1 and 2 on their vital parts and having regard to the 
medical evidence on record, the injuries suffered by PW .1 and the 
deceased, we are not inclined to accept the submission of learned 
Counsel for the accused that the offence falls under First Part of 
Section 304 of IPC.” 
 
6. Mr. A. Sirajudeen, the learned senior counsel for the appellants 
confined his argument s to the question whether the appellants are 
liable for conviction for murder or culpable homicide not amounting 
to murder. The learned senior counsel contended that the incident 
took place without premeditation and the injur ies caused to the 
deceased were abrasions and swelling which do not reflect the 
intention of the appellants to commit murder. On the other hand,  
Ms. Rooh-e-hina Dua, the learned State counsel contended that even 
if the incident took place on a trivial issue the injuries have  been 
caused by the appellants on the vital part s of the body. The learned 
State counsel referred to the judgment in  Singapagu Anjaiah v. State 
of Andhra Pradesh 1 and Pulicherla Nagaraju alias Nagaraja Reddy  v. 
State of Andhra Pradesh 2 and contended that the intention of the 
appellants to commit murder can be easily gathered from the fact that 
                                            
1 Singapagu Anjaiah v. State of Andhra Pradesh : (2010) 9 SCC 799 
2 Pulicherla Nagaraju alias Nagaraja Reddy : (2006) 11 SCC 444 

--- Page 174 ---
 
Page 5 of 8 
 
they assaulted Mahendra on his head which caused his death. The 
learned State counsel referred to the internal injuries over the  
parieto-temporal, occipital area and depressed fractured inside the 
brain and submitted that the appellants have rightly been convicted 
under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and 
there is no scope for interference in this Criminal Appeal against t he 
concurrent findings recorded by two Courts.  
7. We have considered the rival submissions and perused the 
materials on record. The prosecution witnesses admitted in the Court 
that there was a dispute between two families for last 10 years  
for drawing water through the channel. PW2 admitted in the 
cross-examination that there have been quarrel for the same reason 
in the past and the parties had agreed  to end the dispute o n 
compromise. This is also an admission by PW1 in the Court that he 
was addicted to drinking and would take alcohol every day. However, 
he denied the suggestion put to him on behalf of the defence that he 
used to pick up quarrels with the villagers after consuming alcohol. 
8. The incident of 10 th November 2014 started with a quarrel 
which took place around 09:30 PM when PW1 was passing through 
the house of the  appellant No.1. The appellants and the mother of 
Manukumara stopped PW1 and engaged in a quarrel with him 
regarding the flow of water to their land. They assaulted PW1 and 

--- Page 175 ---
 
Page 6 of 8 
 
thrashed him on the ground. In the meantime, PW2 and her son , 
namely, Mahendra intervened to pacify the quarrel but the appellants 
assaulted them also. This is the case of the prosecution that the 
appellants assaulted the deceased with a wooden stick, which at some 
places is described as firewood also. Quite clearly, assault upon the 
deceased was not premeditated inasmuch as he was not present on 
the spot when a quarrel started between the appellant s and PW1. It 
was at the spur of the moment that the appellants assaulted the 
deceased with a wooden stick. The deceased succumbed to the 
injuries the next da y in the course of the treatment. This fact is, 
therefore, referable to the nature of injuries caused by the appellants 
and assumes significance for examining the nature of offence 
committed by them.  
9. Exception 4 to section 300 of the Indian Penal Code is attracted 
and the accused escapes his conviction for murder where it is 
established from the materials on record that injury was caused in a 
sudden fight and without any premeditation. This should be inferred 
from the materials on record that the assault on the victim came in 
the heat of passion and the accused did not take any undue advantage 
or acted in a cruel manner.  This is also required to be kept in mind 
that the number of injuries caused to the victim is not a decisive factor 
and what is important is that the incident happened suddenly and 

--- Page 176 ---
 
Page 7 of 8 
 
without any premeditation (see, Surinder Kumar v. Union Territory, 
Chandigarh3).  The internal injuries which were in the nature of 
contusions and depressed fractures may become aggravating 
circumstance for convicting the accused for murder, provided the 
prosecution is able to prove that the evidence produced b y it brings 
that case under one of the four clauses under section 300 of the 
Indian Penal Code and that the accused is not entitled to any benefit 
under the Exceptions provided thereunder. 
10. In our considered opinion, the appellants are not liable to be 
convicted under section 302/34 of the Indian Penal Code for causing 
death of Mahendra. Both the Courts failed to take note of the genesis 
of the occurrence. Out of five external injuries found on the dead body 
of Mahendra, four of them were on left cheek, upper part of neck, 
upper part of the chest and left forearm. It was the injury  
No. 2 found over the left frontal head that caused the internal injuries 
due to which Mahendra died. Now in this factual scenario, it must be 
held that the evidence brought on record by the prosecution was not 
sufficient to  prove the charge under section 302 read with section 34 
of the Indian  Penal Code. Therefore, the conviction and sentence of 
the appellants for the said charge are set aside. The appellants are, 
however, convicted under section 304 Part I of the Indian Penal Code. 
                                            
3 Surinder Kumar v. Union Territory, Chandigarh : (1989) 2 SCC 217 

--- Page 177 ---
 
Page 8 of 8 
 
We are informed that the appellants have undergone actual sen tence 
of more than 9 years and, in view thereof, they are sentenced to period 
already undergone by them with fine of Rs.5,000/ - each. The 
conviction and sentence of the appellants under sections 307 and 341 
both read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code are maintained. 
11. This Criminal Appeal is partly allowed in the aforesaid terms. 
The appellants shall be released forthwith, if they are not in custody 
in connection with any other case.

IA NO.317864/2026 AND IA NO.317866/2026:
1. The learned counsel appearing for the petitioner(s) submits
that spanning across 20 districts, there were 264 under-trial
prisoners who have been granted bail. They could not be
released  for  want  of  execution  of  sureties,  and  other
conditions imposed by the concerned Trial Courts.
2. Mr. Pradeep Mishra, the learned Senior counsel appearing for
the State of Uttar Pradesh (U.P.) submits that out of 264
under-trial prisoners, only 158 have been released and an
appropriate  decision  will  be  taken  with  respect  to  106
prisoners. 
3. The learned counsel appearing for the National Legal Services
Authority (‘NALSA’) submits that periodical reviews have been
undertaken every month with the active participation of the
District Legal Services Authorities. The cases which have not
been dealt with, would be added in the meeting which is to be

--- Page 184 ---
7
convened next month. That is the reason why there are still
106 under-trial prisoners who are yet to be released. 
4. The learned Senior counsel appearing for the petitioner(s)
further submitted that the statistics available are only with
respect to 20 districts, and therefore, the said exercise has
to be undertaken for the remaining 55 districts.
5. The learned Senior counsel appearing for the State of U.P.
submits that the needful would be done within a reasonable
time. 
6. Taking note of the submissions made, we direct the State of
U.P to undertake the exercise for the under-trial prisoners
who have been granted bail but could not be released for want
of compliance of conditions of bail, in consultation with the
respective District Legal Service Authorities. 
7. This direction shall be applicable even to those under-trial
prisoners who could not comply with the bail conditions,
despite the fact that they have engaged the private lawyers.
There cannot be any differentiation between the under-trial
prisoners, who have the assistance of District Legal Services
Authority and those who have engaged private counsel. 
8. The fact remains that both the categories are similar with
respect to non-compliance of the bail conditions imposed.
Merely because the private lawyers have been engaged, the
assistance from the District Legal Services Authority counsel
cannot be denied and also the benefit that has been extended
to such of persons who have already been rendered assistance

--- Page 185 ---
8
by the District Legal Services Authorities. Litigation cannot
be adversarial in that sense. Therefore, notwithstanding the
presence of counsel appearing for the accused person who have
been granted bail, further assistance can be rendered by the
District Legal Services Authorities to them. In any case, the
onus lies on the State to make sure that these persons are
released from custody. We also request the concerned Courts to
take up those cases which were brought into notice by the
respective District Legal Services Authorities and modify the
condition(s) suitably, so that the under-trial prisoners can
be released accordingly.
9. List on 20.01.2027. 
10. Needless to state that the aforementioned directions shall
apply to all the under-trial prisoners spanning across 75
districts.

  IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NOS.         OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP (Crl.) Nos.14089-14091 OF 2026)
BASANTA DEHURY ETC.               ...APPELLANT(S) 
VERSUS
THE STATE OF ORISSA      ….RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
Leave granted.
2. Briefly stated, the facts of the case are that on
09.10.2014, the appellants herein are alleged to have
entered the home of the deceased at about 9:00 PM,
dragged them out of their home and inflicted blows upon
them by way of sharp weapons, beheaded them and carried
their heads for some distance before throwing them onto
the road. The two minor children of the deceased bore
witness  to  the  entire  incident.  An  FIR  bearing  No.
44/2014 came to be lodged at P.S Nayakote, District
Keonjhar under Sections 302 and 450 read with 34 of the
Indian Penal Code, 1860 (hereinafter, “IPC”) in respect
of the said incident. By judgment dated 31.08.2020, the
Additional  Sessions  Judge,  Keonjhar  convicted  the
appellants herein for the said offences in S.T Case No.
1

--- Page 187 ---
26/53 of 2015 and sentenced them to life imprisonment and
to pay a fine of Rs. 10,000/- each for the offence under
Section 302 of the IPC, and rigorous imprisonment for
five years and to pay a fine of Rs. 5,000/- each for the
offence under Section 450 of the IPC, with the sentences
to run concurrently. 
3. Feeling aggrieved, the appellants preferred appeals
against their conviction before the High Court of Orissa
at Cuttack bearing JCRLA No. 37/2020, CRLA No. 416/2021
and CRLA No. 417/2021. By order dated 27.03.2023, the
High Court upheld the conviction of the appellants and
further, issued notice to the appellants as to why their
conviction  should  not  be  enhanced  for  being  non-
commensurate with the gravity of the offence committed.
By the impugned judgment dated 04.08.2023, the High Court
modified the sentence awarded by the Trial Court to add a
rider that the appellants would not be eligible for
remission as per law before undergoing a minimum of
twenty years of imprisonment, and awarded further amounts
as monetary compensation to the minor children of the
deceased. This was on the basis of the brutality of the
crime and the likely impact on the minor children who had
2

--- Page 188 ---
witnessed  the  entire  incident  and  would  likely  have
lifelong trauma as a consequence. 
4. Hence, the instant appeals. 
5. We have heard learned counsel for the appellants and
learned panel counsel for the respondent/State.
6. Learned counsel for the appellants submitted that by
judgment dated 31.08.2020 in S.T. Case No.26/53 of 2015,
learned  Additional  Sessions  Judge,  Keonjhar,  had
convicted  the  appellants  herein  and  had  imposed  the
sentence of life imprisonment and fine. Being aggrieved by
the  said  judgment  of  conviction  and  sentence,  the
appellants herein had preferred JCRLA No.37/2020, CRLA
Nos.416/2021 and 417/2021 before the High Court. The High
Court while dismissing the appeals ought not to have
modified the sentence of life imprisonment imposed on the
appellants herein with a rider that they shall not be
eligible to claim remission as per law before undergoing
a minimum twenty years of imprisonment followed by the
order of compensation. In this context, learned counsel
for the appellants placed reliance on judgment of this
Court in Nagarajan vs. State of Tamil Nadu, (2025) 8 SCC
331 (“Nagarajan”) which followed the earlier judgment of
3

--- Page 189 ---
this Court in Sachin vs. State of Maharashtra, (2025) 9
SCC 507 (“Sachin”) . He therefore, submitted that the
appellants could not have been worse off in their appeals
wherein they had assailed the judgment of conviction and
sentence of life imprisonment imposed on them. According
to learned counsel for the appellants as a result of the
impugned modified sentence imposed by the High Court,
they have also lost their right to seek remission in
accordance with law. Hence, the learned counsel for the
appellant submitted that paragraph 22 of the impugned
judgment may be set aside and the appeals may be allowed.
He further submitted that neither the State nor the
victims had preferred any criminal appeal(s) and hence in
the appellants’ appeals, there could not have been a
modification of their sentence to their prejudice; That
the High Court could have very well dismissed the appeals
in case it was not inclined to interfere in the judgment
and sentence imposed by the Trial Court.
7. Per contra, learned panel counsel appearing for the
State of Orissa supported the impugned judgment  and
vehemently contended that the grievous nature of the
crime committed by the appellants herein demanding such a
4

--- Page 190 ---
sentence to be imposed and the High Court was justified
in doing so; that the imposition of life sentence was not
sufficient and hence the Constitution Court exercising
its appellate jurisdiction rightly imposed the sentence
as stated in paragraph 22 of the impugned judgment.
Hence, there is no merits in these appeals.
8. We have considered the arguments advanced at the Bar.
The bone of contention between the parties is what is
stated by the High Court in paragraph 22 of the impugned
judgment which for ease of reference is extracted as
under:
“22. In the result, the order of sentence
passed by the trial Court is hereby modified
and  the  appellants  are  sentenced  to
imprisonment for life with the rider that they
shall not be eligible to claim remission as per
law before undergoing a minimum 20 years of
imprisonment  followed  by  the  order  of
compensation as aforesaid.” 
9. We note that the appellants, who are the accused had
preferred  the  appeals  assailing  the  judgment  of
conviction as well as sentence of life imprisonment and
fine imposed on them by the Trial Court before the High
Court.  There was no other appeal or revision filed
either by the State or the victims.  In the absence of
5

--- Page 191 ---
there being such cases filed, in the appeals filed by the
appellants herein, the High Court ought not to have
enhanced the sentence.  The jurisdiction of the High
Court was only with regard to the consideration of the
judgment of the Trial Court on merits. In this regard, we
take note of Section 386 (b)(ii) of the Code of Criminal
Procedure, 1973 which reads as under:
“386. Powers of the Appellate Court - 
xxx
(b) In an appeal from a conviction -
xxx
(ii)  with  or  without  altering  the  finding,
alter the nature or the extent, or the nature
and extent, of the sentence, but not so as to
enhance the same.”
10. We also place reliance on our judgments in the case
of Sachin as well as Nagarajan.
11. Consequently, we set aside the sentence imposed by
the  High  Court  and  restore  the  sentence  of  life
imprisonment and fine imposed by the Trial Court.
These appeals are allowed in the aforesaid terms.

impugned order dated 08.07.2026, the appellant

“Issue notice to the respondent,

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
INHERENT JURISDICTION
CONTEMPT PETITION (CIVIL) NO. 193/2025
in
CIVIL APPEAL NO. 7932/2024
E GLOBETECH INDIA PVT. LTD. ..... PETITIONER(S)
VERSUS
DEORANJAN KUMAR SINGH & ORS. ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. This contempt case was instituted alleging willful disobedience
to the order dated 23.07.2024 passed by this Court in Civil
Appeal No. 7932/2024.  By the said order, this Court allowed
the appeal and directed that payments made by the petitioner,
E Globetech India Pvt. Ltd., should be refunded to it by the
State of Odisha within a period of six weeks from the date of
receipt of a copy of the said order.  Similarly, the securities
furnished and the amounts deposited by Ajit Kumar Sahu, the
appellant in Civil Appeal No. 7932/2024, were also directed to
be refunded to him within a period of six weeks from the date
of receipt of a copy of the said order by the State of Odisha.
2. Compliance having been reported by the respondents/alleged
contemnors,  viz.  Deoranjan  Kumar  Singh,  Additional  Chief
Secretary, Revenue and Disaster Management Department, State of
Odisha;  Somesh  Kumar  Upadhyay,  Collector  and  District
Cont. Pet. (C) No. 193/2025     1

--- Page 202 ---
Magistrate,  Dhenkanal;  and  Satyajit  Mohapatra,  Tehsildar,
Gondia,  Dhenkanal,  this  Court  noted  that  there  was  no
explanation  for  the  delay  in  such  compliance  and,  on
17.07.2026,  called  upon  the  named  respondents/alleged
contemnors to file individual affidavits explaining the delay
on the part of each of them in abiding by the time stipulation
in the order dated 23.07.2024.
3. Pursuant thereto, affidavit dated 04.08.2026 was filed only by
Ashish  Ishwar  Patil,  the  present  Collector  and  District
Magistrate, Dhenkanal, wherein he sought to explain the delay.
4. It is an admitted fact, as is evident from the aforestated
affidavit dated 04.08.2026, that the certified copy of the
order dated 23.07.2024 passed by this Court in Civil Appeal No.
7932/2024 was received by the authorities on 24.09.2024. The
steps taken thereafter, as set out in the aforestated affidavit
dated 04.08.2026, clearly reflect the play of bureaucratic red
tape and paper-pushing by the authorities concerned. It is also
an admitted fact that no steps were taken by any of the
authorities concerned to seek extension of time when they were
not in a position to comply with the time stipulation fixed by
this Court in its order dated 23.07.2024.  
5. As noted earlier, the certified copy of the order was received
on 24.09.2024 but the refunds pursuant thereto were effected
only from 07.12.2024, long after the expiry of six weeks’
period stipulated by this Court. Worse, we find that such
refunds spilled over to the next year also, as the substantial
Cont. Pet. (C) No. 193/2025     2

--- Page 203 ---
amount  of  40,37,084/-  (Rupees  forty  lakhs  thirty  seven₹
thousand eighty four only) was refunded only on 05.08.2025.
Further, refund of the stamp duty and the cost of the mining
plan  quantified  at  3,40,420/-  (Rupees  three  lakhs  forty₹
thousand  four  hundred  twenty  only)  was  released  only  on
03.07.2026.  In all, 77,04,762/- (Rupees seventy seven lakhs₹
four thousand seven hundred sixty two only) is stated to have
been refunded but interest was paid only on two of the heads,
totaling just over 26,00,000/- (Rupees twenty six lakhs only)₹
out of the total amount of 77,04,762/- (Rupees seventy seven₹
lakhs four thousand seven hundred sixty two only).  
6. As there was no direction by this Court as to payment of
interest, it is not within the scope of this Court in exercise
of contempt jurisdiction to address any such claim in relation
to the delayed refund.  
7. However, we must take serious note of the lengthy delay on the
part of the authorities in complying with the order passed by
this Court, despite a clear stipulation therein with regard to
the time period within which the order was to be implemented.
To compound the same, the authorities did not even take steps
to seek extension of time upon realizing that they would not be
able to comply with the temporal mandate of the order dated
23.07.2024. This careless disregard and lack of diligence
towards Court directions and more so, with regard to time
frames within which the said directions should be complied
with, has become the norm rather than an exception. The
Cont. Pet. (C) No. 193/2025     3

--- Page 204 ---
authorities  then  conveniently  blame  administrative  and
bureaucratic delays to account for the lapse on their part in
sticking to the time frame fixed by the Court.  The least that
is expected of such authorities is to approach the Court for
extension of time in those circumstances.  
8. Complete disregard and nonchalance towards the temporal mandate
fixed by this Court in the order dated 23.07.2024 by the
authorities  concerned  is  manifest  in  the  present  case.
Permitting authorities to ignore such time stipulations with
impunity would send out a wrong signal and perpetuate this
distressing propensity on their part to simply ignore time
stipulations and walk away unscathed, citing the time consumed
in the bureaucratic paper-pushing that they have indulged in,
as is evident from the affidavit dated 04.08.2026.  
9. In these circumstances, we are constrained to impose costs upon
the State of Odisha to set an example, so as to obviate this
kind of attitude and approach at least in future.  
10. The contempt case is, therefore, amenable to closure recording
the delayed compliance with the directions of this Court in the
order dated 23.07.2024 in Civil Appeal No. 7932/2024. However,
in view of the delay on the part of the State of Odisha and its
authorities in doing so, the State of Odisha shall pay costs of

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION
TRANSFER PETITION(S) (CIVIL) No(S).2221 of 2026
SAI  MAGHALAKSHMI  TRADERS  &
ORS.            .....PETITIIONER(S) 
VERSUS
M/S SRI LAKSHMI SRINIVASA AGRO FOODS 
& ANR.         .....RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. This Transfer Petition is filed by the petitioners seeking the
following reliefs:
“Transfer  CS(COMM)  625/2026  titled  “M/s.  Sri
Lakshmi  Srinivasa  Agro  Foods  &  Anr.  v.  Sai
Maghalakshmi  Traders  &  Ors.”  together  with  all
pending  applications  therein,  from  the  file  of  the
Hon’ble High Court of Delhi at New Delhi to the file of
the Hon’ble High Court of Judicature at Madras for
trial and disposal in accordance with law.”
2. We have heard learned counsel for the petitioners and learned
counsel for the respondents.
1

--- Page 220 ---
3. We find that the petitioners herein, who are the defendants in
the suit, are carrying on business at Chennai and the respondents
herein, who are the plaintiffs, have their principal place of business
at Nelmangala, Bangalore Rural District, Karnataka. 
4. We fail to understand as to why the respondents/plaintiffs
have  filed  the  suit  before  the  Delhi  High  Court  when  both  the
parties are residing in the neighbouring States of Karnataka and
Tamil  Nadu  and  the  Madras  High  Court  also  has  original
jurisdiction to entertain the suit.
5. We  wish  to  observe  that  it  is  not  merely  concerns  of
convenience that animate the need for transfer of proceedings in the
instant case. While it could be true that various High Courts may
have the jurisdiction to hear a particular case, especially in the case
of intellectual property disputes, any perception of a particular High
Court being better suited to hearing a particular type of dispute is
entirely misguided and erroneous. The mere existence of territorial
jurisdiction in various courts cannot on its own become justification
for forum shopping and cannot result in the perpetuation of notions
2

--- Page 221 ---
of a hierarchy among the High Courts of this country. We also wish
to highlight that, ordinarily, in a case whose respective parties,
genesis and factual locus are based in a particular location, the
courts of the said location would be most suited to understanding
the nuances of that case.
6.  We therefore, find that the petitioner has made out a case for
transfer of the suit from the Delhi High Court to the Madras High
Court. We also find that the interests of justice would be served in
the instant  case, having  regard to the fact that the parties are
carrying on their respective businesses in the neighbouring States
of Karnataka and Tamil Nadu and therefore for the expediency of
disposal and bearing in mind all practical aspects, the Transfer
Petition is liable to be allowed. 
7.  Accordingly, the Transfer Petition is allowed and the case viz.,
CS(COMM) 625/2026 on the file of the High Court of Delhi at New
Delhi is transferred to the High Court of Judicature at Madras. 
3

--- Page 222 ---
8.  The respondents are at liberty to appear before the Transferee
Court either in person or through video conferencing facility. 
..........................................,J.
(B.V. NAGARATHNA)
..........................................,J.
(R. MAHADEVAN)
NEW DELHI
OCTOBER 28, 2026.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL No.5261 OF 2026
[arising out of SLP (Crl.) No.14154 OF 2026]
SHAMSHU JAMA @ SHAMSUL ZAMA 
@ S ZAMA      APPELLANT
VERSUS
THE STATE OF BIHAR            RESPONDENT
 
O R D E R 
1. Leave granted.
2. The  High Court of Judicature  at Patna, by the
impugned judgment and order dated 09 th July, 2026,
has  rejected  the  appellant’s  prayer  for  bail  in
anticipation of arrest. 
3. Appellant figures as an accused in FIR No. 322
dated  20th June,  2025  registered  at  Police  Station
Sakra,  District  Muzaffarpur,  Bihar  under  Sections
Criminal Appeal No.5261 OF 2026 1

--- Page 226 ---
126(2), 115, 118, 117, 109 & 3(5) of the Bharatiya
Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
4. We  have  heard  learned  counsel  appearing  for
the parties as well as perused the counter affidavit
filed by the respondent-State.
5. It appears from such affidavit that though the
appellant figures as an accused in FIR No. 322/2025,
there is a previous FIR, viz. FIR No.313/2025, wherein
the victim figured as an accused. It is, therefore, clear
that cross cases have been registered.
6. Be that as it may, the postmortem report records
that death of the victim was due to “lung disease”.
7. Insofar as the injury on the victim is concerned,
the report further concludes that there appears to be
an injury on the long bone on his right arm.
8. T aking an overall view of the matter but without
expressing any opinion either way on the cause of
death,  we  are  of  the  considered  opinion  that the
appellant’s detention for custodial interrogation is not
necessary and that he may be admitted to an order
Criminal Appeal No.5261 OF 2026 2

--- Page 227 ---
for grant of bail in anticipation of arrest.
9. We,  accordingly,  set  aside  the  judgment  and
order impugned in this appeal.
10. It is directed that in the event of the appellant
being arrested, he shall be released on bail on terms
and conditions to be imposed by the trial court.

O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. This appeal arises from the order passed by the High
Court  dated  21.10.2024  in  Criminal  Revision  Petition
No.990 of 2016 by which the Revision Petition preferred by
the appellant herein, original accused came to be partly
allowed to the extent of reducing the sentence imposed by
the Trial Court.
3. It appears from the materials on record that the
appellant was put to trial in the Court of the Civil Judge
and JMFC, Belthangady in Criminal Case No.770 of 2009 for
the offence punishable under Section 304A of the Indian
Penal  Code  (for  short,  ‘the  IPC’),  i.e.,  rash  and
negligent act.
4. The Trial Court held the appellant guilty of the
alleged offence and sentenced him to undergo one year of
simple imprisonment with fine of Rs.1,000/-.
5. The appellant, being dissatisfied with the judgment
and order of conviction and sentence passed by the Trial
1

--- Page 238 ---
Court, went in appeal before the Sessions Court. The
Sessions Court dismissed the appeal and, thereby affirmed
the judgment and order of conviction passed by the Trial
Court.
6. Thereafter, the appellant went before the High Court
by way of a Revision Petition. The High Court, in exercise
of its revisional jurisdiction thought fit to affirm the
order of conviction, however, reduced the sentence from
one year simple imprisonment to six months of simple
imprisonment but at the same time, enhanced the fine
amount by Rs.25,000/-.
7. In  such  circumstances  referred  to  above,  the
appellant is here before us with the present appeal.
8. We  heard  the  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the
parties.
9. It appears that the incident in question occurred on
26.08.2009. The appellant was serving as a driver of a
private bus by name ‘Vishal’. On the fateful day and date
of  the  incident,  while  entering  the  bus  stand,  the
appellant is alleged to have knocked down a motorcyclist,
resulting in the death of the rider of the motorcycle.
10. To put it briefly, it is the case of the prosecution
that the appellant was driving his bus in a very rash and
negligent manner which led to this accident, resulting in
the death of the rider of the motorcycle.
11. It appears from the materials on record that the
2

--- Page 239 ---
pillion  rider  on  motorcycle  was  the  father  of  the
deceased.
12. Having regard to the fact that the incident is of the
year 2009 and also taking into consideration the age of
the appellant as on date, which we are informed is 65, we
would like to grant some indulgence to the appellant.
13. We  are  inclined  to  reduce  the  sentence  of  the
appellant from six months simple imprisonment to one week
of simple imprisonment. However, at the same time, we
direct the appellant to pay an amount of Rs.2,00,000/-
(Rupees Two Lakh only) by way of compensation to the
family of the victim within a period of eight weeks from
today.
14. The appellant shall surrender within a period of two
weeks from today before the Trial Court. The Trial Court,
upon surrender, shall take the appellant in custody for
the  purpose  of  serving  out  the  sentence  of  simple
imprisonment of one week.
15. The amount of Rs.75,000/- along with interest which
has already been deposited with the Registry of this Court
shall be now disbursed in favour of the family of the
victim.
16. The  District  Legal  Services  Authority,  Bengaluru,
State  of  Karnataka  shall  ensure  that  the  amount  of
Rs.75,000/- along with interest deposited by the appellant
with the Registry of this Court is disbursed in favour of
3

--- Page 240 ---
the family of the victim and the enhanced amount of
compensation awarded by us today is also paid to the
family of the deceased, within a period of eight weeks
from today.
17. The appeal stands disposed of in the aforesaid terms.
18. Pending  application(s),  if  any,  shall  also  stand
disposed of.

SLP (Crl.) No.17653/2026                            1

Raju Kumar causing injuries.

thrash out the dispute including the refund of the amount paid by the
complainant to the appellant/accused. Pursuant to the same, the wisdom
seems to have dawned upon the parties and appellant/accused is said to
have paid the entire amount received from complainant. That apart, a
further sum of Rs.4 Lakhs, is said to have been paid by the appellant to
the complainant, which the learned counsel appearing for Respondent
No.2 does not dispute or in other words acknowledge the receipt of the
same.
5. It is in this background IA No.203448/2026 has been filed under Article
142 of the Constitution of India for quashing of the pending FIR and all
proceedings pursuant thereto.
6.  Having  regard  to  the  nature  of  transaction  and  both  the  parties,
namely,  the  Appellant  and  the  Respondent  No.2-complainant,  having
resolved  their  dispute,  namely,  the  complainant  having  receiving  the
entire  amount  paid  by  him  to  the  appellant/accused  along  with  an
additional sum of Rs.4 Lakhs, we are of the considered view, continuation
of the criminal prosecution, would only be a waste of precious judicial
time and it would not serve any purpose.  Hence, in this background, we
proceed to pass the following order.
7.  The  appeal  is  allowed.  All  proceedings  initiated  pursuant  to  the
registration  of  FIR  No.27/2025  by  the  Police  Station  Sadar,  District
                                                                       2                                                                            

--- Page 257 ---
Pathankot, for the offence punishable under Section 420 of the Indian
Penal Code, 1860 (IPC), stands quashed.
8. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand consigned to records.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
MISCELLANEOUS APPLICATION DIARY NO.1730/2023
IN
C.A. NO.  8047/2022
YOGEGOWDA(D) TR.LRS.                               APPLICANT(S)
                                VERSUS
CHANNEGOWDA (D) THR.LRS..                          RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. The applications for setting aside the abatement and for
substitution are allowed.
2. Cause title be amended accordingly. 
3. The present miscellaneous application has been filed
seeking  recall  of  judgment  dated  01.11.2022  in  Civil  Appeal
No.8047/2022 by the applicants, who were the respondents therein.
Aggrieved by the disposal of the appeal in view of a Memorandum of
Compromise dated 18.10.2022, the applicants are before this Court.
4. We have heard the learned counsel appearing for the
parties. 
5. Admittedly, the applicants being party-respondent(s) in
the Civil Appeal, though did not appear before this Court, were not

--- Page 266 ---
2
made parties to the Memorandum of Compromise. 
6. The compromise is binding on the other parties in the
Civil Appeal, as they were a party to it. The difficulty that
arises is that it cannot be given effect to unless the applicant(s)
agree  upon  the  terms  of  Memorandum  of  Compromise.  As  the
applicant(s) were not a party to the memorandum of compromise and
hence, they do not agree with the terms agreed upon thereunder.
7. In such view of the matter, we have no other option
except to set aside the judgment dated 01.11.2022, which leads to
setting aside the compromise inter se parties qua the share of the
applicant(s). 
8. Accordingly, the order dated 01.11.2022 stands set aside
and the appeal stands restored to its original file. 
9. IA No. 8057/2023 stands allowed and the Miscellaneous
Application stands disposed of.

5. The allegation against the appellant is that he had

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NOS.             OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP (C)No. 17355-17356 of 2026)
ANASAVVA W/O  TIPPANAGOUDA BHARAMAGOUDRA & ORS. APPELLANT(S)
                                VERSUS
MADEVI & ORS.                                  RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R 
1. Leave granted.
2. The challenge in these appeals is to the order dated
23.03.2026 passed by the High Court of Karnataka dismissing
the First Appeals of the appellants under Section 96 of the
CPC on the ground of delay of 145 days in filing the
appeals. As the application(s) justifying and assigning the
delay was dismissed, the appeals were consequently dismissed
as well.
3. Having  considered  the  submissions  of  the  learned
counsel for the parties, on perusal of the records, and the
application for condonation of delay, we are inclined to
accept the appellants' prayer, as we find the delay was
reasonably explained before the High Court in the First
Appeals.
1

--- Page 320 ---
4. Learned counsel for the appellants further submits that
the Suit was for partition and it being First Appeal, the
opportunity should have been given to the appellants to
agitate the case on merits.  Both these submissions as made
by the learned counsel for the appellants on the basis of
the records, appear to be correct and we accept the same.
Despite the opposition made by the learned counsel for the
respondent(s), we are unable to agree with him as the
primary intent especially in First Appeal(s) of the Courts
should be to decide the case on merits instead of relying on
technical reasons for smothering the process of appeal(s)
without reverting to the merits.
5. In the light of the above, we set aside the impugned
order dated 23.03.2026 passed by the High Court in RFA
No.100375/2024 (PAR/POS) and RFA No. 100376/2024 and allow
the application(s) filed by the appellant(s) for condonation
of delay, before the High Court.  The delay stands condoned
in filing of the First Appeals. The Regular First Appeals
are restored to their original numbers.
6. Parties are directed to appear before the High Court on
4th December, 2026.
7. We request the High Court to make an endeavour to
decide  the  appeals  at  an  early  date.  In  case  the
jurisdiction  has been transferred to some other Court, the
2

--- Page 321 ---
file(s)  be  accordingly  transmitted  to  the  said
jurisdictional Court for decision.
8. With the above observations, appeals are allowed.
9. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

anticipatory bail.

ordered  to  be  released  on  anticipatory  bail  by  the  jurisdictional

appellant cooperating with the investigation.

                             O R D E R
SLP(Crl) No. 15832/2026 
Leave granted.
IA No. 254598/2026 in Criminal Appeal No(s). 4082/2026 - SUSPENSION
OF SENTENCE
1. We have heard the learned Senior Counsel appearing for the
applicant as well as the learned Solicitor General, learned
Additional Solicitor General and the learned Advocate General
appearing for the respondent – State.
2. Learned Senior Counsel appearing for the applicant submitted
that it is a case where the High Court has reversed the
acquittal rendered by the Trial Court. The Trial Court has

--- Page 333 ---
3
considered the evidence in extenso and disbelieved the case of
the prosecution, particularly, that of the prosecutrix.
3. It is further submitted that the evidence with respect to CCTV
footage and the fact that the concerned lift in which the
occurrence is stated to have happened opens automatically,
whenever  it  stops,  have  not  been  duly  taken  into
consideration.  Even  according  to  the  prosecution,  the
occurrence is stated to have happened within a short span of
time.  The  evidence  of  PW-4  disputes  the  case  of  the
prosecution. 
4. It is also submitted that the applicant was in custody pending
trial as well, and has been under incarceration for a total
period of nine months. He is not a flight risk. Considering
the above, a fervent plea has been made to suspend the
sentence of the applicant.
5. Learned Solicitor General and the learned Additional Solicitor
General appearing for the respondent – State, while opposing
the application for suspension of sentence, submitted that the
High Court has considered the evidence  in extenso. A Special
Leave Petition, being SLP (Crl.) No. 15832/2026,  has been
filed by the respondent – State seeking enhancement of the
sentence imposed on the applicant. The High Court has rightly
observed that the Trial Court has put the prosecutrix on
trial, as against the applicant.  
6. It is further submitted that the apology emails, coupled with
the text messages sent by the applicant, if read along with
the ocular version of the prosecution witnesses, would clearly

--- Page 334 ---
4
show that the occurrence has happened, as projected by the
prosecution. Inasmuch as the High Court has considered the
relevant material, it is submitted there is no need for
suspension of the applicant’s sentence at this stage.
7. Having heard the parties, we are, at the moment, concerned
with the suspension of sentence of the applicant. Though, it
is contended on behalf of the applicant that the Trial Court
has  considered  the  material  available  on  record  while
rendering an acquittal, on a prima facie view, particularly,
with respect to the evidence adduced by the prosecution
witnesses, read with the material produced on record with
specific reference to the apology emails and text message(s),
we do not find that it is a fit case for grant of suspension
of sentence.
8. The fact remains that the prosecutrix was working under the
applicant. The father of the prosecutrix and the applicant
were friends. Similarly, the prosecutrix and the daughter of
the applicant were also friends.  
9. From the above, we cannot say that there was a motive on the
part of the prosecutrix to implicate the applicant.
10.In such view of the matter, on a  prima facie view, we are not
inclined to suspend the sentence of the applicant.
11.Accordingly, the application stands dismissed.
12.List the appeals for hearing in their due course
(ASHA SUNDRIYAL)                                (POONAM VAID)

1. Leave granted.
2. In pursuance of the order passed by this Court
on 02.09.2026, the compliance affidavit has been
filed by the appellant.
3. We are inclined to record paragraph 6 of the
same as under:
“6. The wordmark SPMGOPAL registered by the
petitioner is very much different from the trade
mark registered and used by the respondent No.2
and the trademark has to read as a whole.
However,  in  contravention  of  the  said
provisions, not only the deponent was arrested
but search and seizure of the articles had been
carried out by the ASI not being competent to
carry out investigation, at the work place and
shops of the customers of the deponent.  This
has caused a huge financial, mental and social
loss to the deponent and under the compelling
circumstances,  the  deponent  has  shut  the
business of his SPM Food products. The deponent
has already sold the machinery and even a public

--- Page 336 ---
2
notice dated 01.01.2025 has been published by
the deponent in Hindi NEWS PAPER PUNJAB KESARI
to the effect that the company has closed for
two years and owner of the company is not
responsible, if any notice is issued to the
company.  On  account  of  non-usage  of  the
trademark SPM GOPAL, the registrar has abandoned
his trademark. At this stage, the deponent has
no intentions and plans to restart the business
of SPM Food Products. The online screenshot of
the  trademark  registered  by  the  petitioner,
searched on 17.04.2026, is already on record as
Annexure P-16 and the true translated copy of
the public notice and newspaper cutting dated
01.01.2025 is Annexure P-17.”
4. The  learned  counsel  appearing  for  the
respondent, by placing reliance upon the response
affidavit, submits that it has to be clarified that
the said compliance is to be considered for the
future as well.
5. The learned counsel appearing for the appellant
has no objection to the aforesaid submission made by
the respondent.
6. In such view of the matter, the appeal stands
disposed  of,  by  taking  note  of  the  aforesaid
affidavit, along with the statement made by the
learned counsel, that the appellant or any of his
assignees would not use the trade mark name,  namely,

--- Page 337 ---
3
SPM GOPAL or GOPAL henceforth.
7. Furthermore,  the  statement  of  the  learned
counsel  appearing  for  the  appellant  that  the
concerned company has been closed and a public notice
has  also  been  published  dated  01.01.2025  stands
recorded.
8. In view of the above, the impugned order stands
set aside and, consequently, the criminal proceedings
arising out of FIR No.61/2020, dated 01.07.2020,
registered at Bhagwantpur, Rupnagar, Punjab, stands
quashed.
9. The civil suit being CS No.91/2019 or any other
suit  inter se  parties touching upon the subject
matter of the present appeal is also directed to be
withdrawn.
10. The appeal stands disposed of, accordingly.
11. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand
disposed of.

O R D E R
1. Read the office report dated 04th November, 2026.
2. Despite service of notice of this transfer petition under Section 25
of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 presented by Ritu Ankitkumar
Patel (hereafter the petitioner) on Ankitkumar Amrutlal Patel (hereafter
the respondent), he has not entered appearance.
3. The  marriage  between the  petitioner  and the  respondent was
solemnized  on  07th December,  2013.  A  boy  child  was  born  to  the
petitioner and the respondent from the wedlock. However, the parties
have since drifted apart owing to differences arising by and between
them.
4. The respondent has instituted proceedings under Section 9 of the
Hindu Marriage Act, 1955, bearing Family Suit No.66 of 2025 titled
“Ankitkumar Amrutlal Patel Vs. Ritu ” which is pending in the court of
the Principal Judge, Family Court, Patan, Gujarat.
5. On the multiple grounds urged in the petition, the petitioner has
sought for transfer of the aforesaid proceedings from the court of the
Principal Judge, Family Court, Patan, Gujarat to the Family Court, Sangli,
Maharashtra.
1

--- Page 352 ---
6. Since  the  respondent  has  not  controverted  the
statements/averments made in the petition, we are of the view that he
has no serious objection to grant of the prayer for transfer.
7. We  are  also  otherwise  satisfied,  having  regard  to  the
inconvenience the petitioner is likely to face if the proceedings were
continued in the court of Principal Judge, Family Court, Patan, Gujarat
(at  a  distance  of  around  1012  kms.  from  her  present  place  of
residence), that interest of justice demands grant of the prayer for
transfer.
8. Hence, the transfer petition is allowed. Family Suit No.66 of 2025
titled “Ankitkumar Amrutlal Patel Vs. Ritu ” pending in the court of the
Principal Judge, Family Court, Patan, Gujarat is transferred to the Family
Court, Sangli, Maharashtra.  Records of Family Suit No.66 of 2025 be
transferred to the transferee court immediately.
9. To avoid delay, the parties are directed to appear before the
transferee court on 07 th December, 2026. If any or both the parties fail
to appear on that day, the presiding officer of the transferee court will
fix another date of appearance. Thereafter, he shall be free to proceed
in accordance with law.
10. The presiding officer shall endeavour to bring about a settlement
between the parties through the process of mediation. If the process is
unsuccessful, nothing shall preclude the presiding officer to take the
proceedings to its logical conclusion on its merits and in accordance
with law.
11. If the respondent is unable to attend the proceedings in person
on any occasion, he will be at liberty to seek permission to attend
2

--- Page 353 ---
through  the  virtual  mode  and  if  such  a  permission  is  sought,  the
presiding officer of the court may proceed to consider it reasonably.
12. Pending application(s), if any, shall also stand disposed of.
